We have discussed the letters of the alphabet (huruf al-hijaʾ, the disjointed letters) at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah. What is specific to "Qaf" is that it has been said: it is from the Name of Allah, al-Qahir (the Subduer) or al-Qadir (the Able). It has also been said: it is a name for the Qur'an.

﴿And the glorious Qur'an﴾ — "al-Majid" is from al-majd, which means honour, nobility and generosity.

The response to this oath is omitted, and its estimated wording is: "They did not refute your command with any proof, nor did they deny you with any evidence," and the like. He expressed this omitted part... The turning away is with "bal" (rather). It has also been said: the response is what is uttered as speech. It has been said: "Indeed in that is a reminder." It has also been said: "We know what the earth diminishes of them." These sayings are weak and forced.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 50, verses 2–3:

﴿Rather, they marvel that a warner has come to them from among themselves.﴾ The pronoun in "they marvel" refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, and the warner is our master Muhammad (ﷺ). It has also been said that the pronoun refers to all people, and Ibn 'Atiyya (Ibn 'Atiyya) chose this view. He said: For this reason, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then the disbelievers said﴾, meaning the disbelievers among mankind. The sound view, however, is that it refers to Quraysh. His saying ﴿Then the disbelievers said﴾ places the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun in order to intend condemning them for disbelief, just as you say: "So-and-so came to me and the wicked man said such-and-such," when you intend to disparage him. His saying ﴿a warner from among them﴾: if the pronoun refers to Quraysh, then the meaning of ﴿from among them﴾ is from their own tribe, so they know his truthfulness, his trustworthiness, and his noble lineage among them. If the pronoun refers to all people, then the meaning of ﴿from among them﴾ is a human being like them. Their marvel may be either that Allah sent a human being as a messenger, or at the matter contained in the warning, which is the Gathering (al-hashr). This is supported by what follows: ﴿When we have died and become dust?﴾ The governing element of "when" (idhā) is omitted, and its estimated form is: "Shall we be resurrected when we have died?" ﴿That is a far return.﴾ "Return" (raj') is a verbal noun from "I returned him" (rajja'tuhu), and what is meant by it is the resurrection after death. The meaning of "far" (ba'id) is far from occurring in their view. It has also been said that "return" means "answer," that is, their answer is far from the truth, and according to this, the saying ﴿That is a far return﴾ is the speech of Allah the Exalted. According to the first view, however, it is a report of the speech of the disbelievers, and this is the more evident.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 50, verse 4:

﴿We certainly know what the earth diminishes of them﴾. This is a response to the disbelievers in their denial of the resurrection. Its meaning: We certainly know what the earth diminishes of them, of their flesh and bones, so resurrecting them is not difficult for Us. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every part of the son of Adam is consumed by the earth, except the coccyx (ʿajb al-dhanab), from which he was created and by which he is reassembled." It was also said: the meaning is, We certainly know what occurs in the depths of the earth of their dead. The first view is the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas and the majority, and it is more apparent. ﴿And with Us is a Book preserved﴾. It means the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz). The meaning of ḥafiẓ (preserved): comprehensive, such that nothing escapes it. It was also said: its meaning is protected from alteration and change.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 50, verse 5:

﴿Nay, they denied the truth when it came to them﴾. This retraction (idrab) is followed by another, the first retraction, to indicate that they have come up with something uglier than their astonishment, namely the denial of the truth, which is prophethood, and what it includes of the report of the resurrection and other things. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this retraction is from a omitted statement, whose estimate is: "They did not examine properly," and the like. ﴿So they are in a confused matter﴾, i.e., in turmoil, because they say: "He is a poet," and at times "a sorcerer," and other such statements of theirs. It was said: its meaning is "rejected." It was said: "confused." It was said: "mixed up."

﴿And We adorned it﴾, meaning with the stars, ﴿and it has no rifts﴾, i.e., no cracks, and this is evidence of the perfection of its craftsmanship. ﴿And We set firm mountains﴾, meaning the mountains, ﴿in it, of every beautiful kind﴾, i.e., of every pleasing type.

﴿And We adorned it﴾, meaning with the stars, ﴿and it has no rifts﴾, i.e., no cracks, and this is evidence of the perfection of its craftsmanship. ﴿And We set firm mountains﴾, meaning the mountains, ﴿in it, of every beautiful kind﴾, i.e., of every pleasing type.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 50, verses 9–11:

﴿Blessed water﴾ means all rain. It is also said: "blessed water" is a particular water that Allah sends down every year, and not every rain is characterized as blessed, but this view is weak. ﴿And grain of the harvest﴾ is wheat, barley and the like, whatever is harvested. ﴿Towering﴾ means tall. ﴿Clusters of date-spathes, piled one upon another﴾: the ṭalʿ (spathe, the first thing that appears of the fruit) is white and layered like pomegranate seeds. As long as it is pressed together, one upon another, it is naḍīd (piled); when it separates, it is no longer naḍīd. ﴿Thus will be the emergence﴾ is an illustration of the emergence of the dead from their graves by the emergence of plants from the earth.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 50, verse 12:

﴿And the companions of the Rass﴾ (ar-Rass): a people who had a great well, and it is the Rass. A prophet was sent to them, but they threw him into the Rass and buried him under earth, and so Allah destroyed them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 50, verses 14–15:

﴿And the companions of al-Ayka﴾ meaning the people of Shu'ayb. The people of Tubba' are mentioned in [Surah al-Dukhan, 37]. ﴿So the promise of My punishment was realized﴾, meaning destruction descended upon them.

﴿Were We then wearied by the first creation?﴾ It is said: "'iya bi-l-amr" (to be unable to know its knowledge) when one does not know its knowledge. The first creation is the creation of man from a drop (nutfah), then from a clot ('alaqah). It is also said: it means the creation of Adam, and it is also said: the creation of the heavens and the earth. The first is more apparent. The purpose of the verse is to argue from the first creation for the resurrection, and the hamza is for denial (istinkar).

﴿Nay, but they are in doubt about a new creation﴾, meaning they are in doubt about the resurrection. The new creation was indefinite because it was not known to the disbelievers being addressed, while the first creation was definite because it was known and familiar.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 50, verse 16:

﴿And We have certainly created man﴾, meaning the species of man. The meaning of ﴿his own self whispers to him﴾ is that his self speaks to him within its thoughts. This is the most hidden of things. It has also been said that it refers to Adam and his whispering when he ate from the tree, but the first (interpretation) is more apparent and more well known. ﴿And We are closer to him than the jugular vein﴾. The (warid) is a large vein in the neck, and there are two veins, one on the right and one on the left. This is a metaphor for extreme nearness, and what is meant by it is the nearness of God's knowledge and His awareness of His servant. The annexation of "habl" (cord) to "warid" (vein) is like your saying "masjid al-jami'" (the congregational mosque). Or it may be that what is meant by "habl" is the shoulder (ʿātiq).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 50, verse 17:

﴿When the two receivers receive﴾ meaning the two angels, the guardians who record the deeds. Talaqqi (receiving) is: receiving the speech by preserving and writing it down. The governing element of "idh" (when) is "nahnu aqrab" (We are closer). It was also said that it is an implied verb whose estimate is: "udhkur" (remember). Ibn 'Atiyya chose this view. ﴿One sitting on the right and one on the left﴾ meaning qa'id (seated): it was also said that qa'id here means maqa'id, in the sense of majalis (sittings), but Ibn 'Atiyya rejected this, arguing that maqa'id is only used with a person's sitting, whereas qa'id applies to every state of a human being. He used the singular while they are two because the estimate is: "'an al-yamin qa'id wa 'an al-shimal qa'id min al-mutalaqqin" (one on the right is a seated one, and one on the left is a seated one, of the receivers), so one of them is omitted because the other indicates it. Al-Farra' said: the word qa'id indicates both the dual and the plural, so no omission is needed.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 50, verse 18:

﴿Not a word does he utter but there is with him a watcher, ready.﴾ Al-ʿatid: the present (al-hadir). In a hadith, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The seat of the two angels is on the two lips; their pen is the tongue and their ink is the saliva." The generality of the verse requires that the two angels record all the deeds of the servant. For this reason al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "They record all speech, then Allah confirms from it the good deeds and the bad deeds and erases the rest." And ʿIkrimah said: "Only the good deeds and the bad deeds are recorded, and nothing else."

And the agony of death comes in truth: that is, with the meeting with God, or the departure from this world. In the codex of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it reads: "And the agony of truth comes with death," and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) recited it likewise. He said "came" in the past tense to affirm the matter and its nearness, and likewise the verbs that follow it. ﴿That is what you used to flee from﴾: that is, you would shy away and run from it. The address is to the human being.

﴿A driver and a witness﴾. The driver (al-sa'iq) is an angel who drives him. As for the witness (al-shahid), it is said that it is another angel who bears witness against him, and this is the most apparent view. It is also said that it is the books of deeds (sahaif al-a'mal), and it is said that it is the person's own limbs (jawarih al-insan).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 50, verse 22:

﴿Indeed, you were in heedlessness of this﴾ is an address to the human being that is implied by His saying "every soul" (kull nafs). He means that he was heedless of what he would encounter in the Hereafter. It has also been said that it is an address to our master Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: you were in heedlessness of this narrative. This is extremely weak, because it departs from the context of the discourse. ﴿So We have removed from you your covering, and your sight today is sharp﴾. It has been said: the removal of the covering is his witnessing the matters of the Hereafter. ﴿Your sight today is sharp﴾, meaning he sees what he did not see before. It has been related: "The people are asleep; when they die, they awaken."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 50, verse 23:

﴿And his companion will say: "This is what is with me, ready."﴾ The companion (al-qarin) here is the devil (shayṭan) who used to lead him astray. It is also said that it is the angel charged with punishing him in Hell, but the first view is more preferred, because he is the companion mentioned afterwards, and because of His saying: ﴿We shall appoint for him a devil, and he will be a companion to him﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 36]. The meaning of His saying: ﴿This is what is with me, ready﴾ is: this person is present with me, whom I have prepared and made ready for Hell. The meaning is the same if we say the companion is the driving angel. And if we say he is one of the guardians of Hell (al-zabaniyya), then its meaning is: this punishment is present with me. It is possible that "mā" in His saying ﴿mā ladayya﴾ is a noun of description (mawsufa) or a relative pronoun (mawsula). If it is a noun of description, then ʿatīd is an adjective describing it. If it is a relative pronoun, then ʿatīd is either a substitute (badal) for it, or a second predicate (khabar baʿd khabar), or the predicate of an omitted subject (khabar mubtada' mahdhuf), and mā is the predicate of the subject under these interpretations. It is also possible that ʿatīd is the predicate, and mā is a substitute (badal) for "hadhā," or is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb (manṣuba bi-fiʿl muḍmar).

"Cast into Hell" — the address is to the two angels, the driver and the witness. It was also said that it is addressed to one person, with the emphatic light nun (al-nun al-mu'akkadah al-khafifah) which was then replaced by an alif; or that its meaning is "Cast, cast," in the dual for intensification and emphasis; or that it follows the habit of the Arabs in addressing two people, as in their saying "khalili" (my two friends) and "sahibi" (my companion). All of this is far-fetched. What indicates that the address is to two is His saying: ﴿So cast him into the severe punishment﴾. ﴿Hindering the good﴾ — it was said: hindering the obligatory zakat; but the sound view is that it is general. ﴿Doubting﴾ — one who is in doubt about the religion; it is from "rayb," meaning doubt. ﴿Who set up﴾ — it may be the subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being ﴿then cast him﴾, and the alif is added to it because it contains the meaning of a condition (shart); or it may be a substitute (badal) or an attribute (sifah), and then "fa-alqiyahu" is a repetition for emphasis.

**﴿His companion will say: "Our Lord, I did not cause him to transgress"﴾** The companion (al-qarīn) here is his devil, who was assigned to him in this world, without any disagreement. The meaning of "I did not cause him to transgress" is: I did not put him into transgression (al-ṭughyān). But he transgressed by his own choice. The waw is omitted here because this is a new, independent sentence (jumla mustaʾnafa, a resumptive clause that begins a fresh statement), unlike His words **﴿And his companion said﴾** before this, which is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with what precedes it, so it takes the waw.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 50, verses 28–30:

﴿Do not dispute before Me.﴾ This is addressed to people and to their companions from the devils. ﴿The word is not changed before Me.﴾ That is, I have already decreed the punishment of the disbelievers, so there is no alteration of that. It was also said: its meaning is that no one lies before Me, since I know all matters. On this view, the reference is to the statement of the companion (qarin), ﴿Our Lord, I did not make him rebellious.﴾ ﴿And it will say, "Is there any more?"﴾ The verb is attributed to Hell (Jahannam). It was also said that it is attributed to its guardians among the angels, and the first is more apparent. Scholars differed over whether Hell speaks literally or figuratively, through the tongue of its state (bi-lisan al-hal). The more apparent view is that it is literal, and that is easy for Allah. The meaning of His words, ﴿Is there any more?﴾, is that it seeks additional [people], while it has not yet been filled. It was also said: "No more," meaning there is no place left in me for additions; on this view it has already been filled. The first is more apparent and preponderant, due to what is narrated in the hadith: "Hell will not cease to have [people] thrown into it, and it will say, 'Is there any more?' until the Almighty places His foot in it," and there is discussion in the hadith that is not the place for it. The word al-mazid may be a verbal noun like al-mahid, or a passive participle. If it is a verbal noun, its pattern is mafil; if it is a passive participle, its pattern is maful.

"And the Garden will be brought near" — i.e., made close. Then he emphasized this by his saying, "not far away." "For every one who turns back (awwab)" — i.e., one who frequently returns to Allah. He is from the verb āba, yaʾūbu, meaning he returned. It was also said: he is one who glorifies Allah, from His saying: ﴿O mountains, echo the praises with him﴾ [Saba': 10]. "Guardian" (ḥafīẓ) — i.e., one who guards the commands of Allah, so he carries them out, and guards against His prohibitions, so he abstains from them.

Those who fear the All-Merciful unseen: ﴿Whoever feared the Most Gracious in the unseen﴾, meaning: who feared God while absent from people. The prepositional phrase (al-majrur) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (al-hal). "Man khashiya" (whoever feared) is either a substitute (badal) or the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada').

If it is asked: how is the name indicating mercy (al-Rahman) joined with fear (al-khashyah)? The answer is that this is intended to emphasize praise of the one who fears God, since he fears Him while knowing His mercy and pardon. Al-Zamakhshari said this. It is also possible that the answer is that "al-Rahman" has come to be used in the manner of a proper name that is not a descriptive attribute, like our saying "Allah."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 50, verse 35:

﴿And with Us is more⁠﻿﴾ It has been said that its meaning is looking at the Face of Allah, as in His saying: ﴿The best reward and more⁠﻿﴾ [Yunus: 26]. It has also been said that it means what has not occurred to their hearts, as is related in the hadith that the Prophet (ﷺ) narrated from his Lord, that He said: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived."

﴿They were mightier than them in strength.﴾ The pronoun in "they" refers to the earlier generations, and in "them" to the disbelievers of Quraysh. ﴿So they roamed through the lands.﴾ That is, they traversed them; the original sense is entering them through their passages (anqab, sing. naqb), or it derives from tanaqqub 'an al-amr (investigating a matter), meaning searching for it. ﴿Was there any escape?﴾ That is, they said: Is there any way of escape from Allah, or from the punishment?

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 50, verses 37–38:

﴿For whoever has a heart﴾ meaning, a heart that is aware, that understands and comprehends. ﴿Or gives ear while he is a witness﴾ meaning, he listens while his heart is present. ﴿And We did not touch by any weariness﴾. Al-lughub (لغوب) is fatigue and exhaustion.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 50, verses 39–40:

﴿So be patient over what they say﴾, meaning the disbelievers of Quraysh and others. ﴿And glorify your Lord with praise﴾. It may mean glorifying with the tongue, or it may mean prayer. al-Zamakhshari mentioned both possibilities. Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is "pray," by the consensus of the interpreters. On this reading it refers to the five daily prayers: ﴿before the rising of the sun﴾ is the dawn prayer (Subh), ﴿and before the setting﴾ is the noon (Zuhr) and afternoon ('Asr) prayers. ﴿And during the night﴾ are the sunset (Maghrib) and night ('Isha') prayers. It has also been said that it refers to the voluntary (nafl) prayers. ﴿And after the prostrations﴾. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: it means the two rak'ahs after Maghrib. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means the voluntary prayers after the obligatory ones. It has also been said: it means the witr prayer.

﴿And listen﴾ means: wait. It governs "the day the caller calls" as a clear direct object (maf'ul bihi). It was also said that the meaning is: listen to what We relate to you of the horrors of the Resurrection. According to this view, it does not govern "the day the caller calls," and one pauses at "listen." The first view is more apparent.

﴿On the day the caller calls from a near place﴾. The caller here is Israfil, who blows the Trumpet (al-Sur). It was said that he is described as near only because all creatures hear him. It was also said that the place is the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and it is described as near because of its nearness to Makkah.

﴿The Day of Emergence﴾ means the people's coming forth from their graves.

﴿يَوْمَ تَشَقَّقُ﴾ The word governing this adverbial phrase of time (al-ʿāmil, the governing element) is the sense of His words ﴿That is a gathering easy for Us﴾, or it is a substitute (badal) for what precedes it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 50, verse 45:

﴿And you are not over them a compeller.﴾ That is, a subduer who forces them to faith, like His saying: ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 22]. It was also said that it is an informing that he (ﷺ) is gentle toward them and not a compeller over them, and this is more apparent. ﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾, like His saying: ﴿You can only warn those who fear their Lord﴾ [Fatir: 18], because reminder benefits only the one who fears.
